mcqs.question: Why can't standard classification metrics like accuracy be directly ported over to evaluate open-ended generated text?
options: Generated text is too long for any metric to process efficiently
There's typically no single correct ground-truth string to compare against, and quality is often multi-dimensional in ways a single label can't capture
Classification metrics only work on numeric data, never text
LLMs cannot produce output that is ever objectively wrong
mcqs.explanation: Classification assumes one correct label per example; generative text often has many valid phrasings and multiple quality dimensions (correctness, tone, safety) that a single right/wrong label can't represent. Length isn't the blocker, classification metrics aren't restricted to numeric data conceptually, and LLM output absolutely can be objectively wrong.

mcqs.question: What is the core limitation of BLEU/ROUGE-style reference-based metrics?
options: They can only be computed on very short texts under 50 words
They require a GPU to compute and are too expensive for most teams
They measure surface-level n-gram overlap with a reference, so a correct but differently-phrased answer can score poorly while a nonsensical answer reusing reference words can score well
They can only be used for classification tasks, never text generation
mcqs.explanation: BLEU/ROUGE compare word-sequence overlap against references, not meaning, so phrasing differences that preserve correctness are penalized while superficial word reuse without real correctness can be rewarded. They're not limited by text length, they're cheap to compute (no GPU needed), and they were designed specifically for generation tasks like translation and summarization.

mcqs.question: An LLM-as-judge consistently rates longer answers higher even when a shorter answer is equally correct. What does this illustrate?
options: LLM judges are useless and should never be used for evaluation
Length bias means the judge is broken and needs to be replaced with BLEU/ROUGE instead
This only happens with judges smaller than the model being evaluated
A documented bias in LLM-judge scoring — favoring surface features like length or confident phrasing — meaning judge scores should be calibrated against human review, not treated as ground truth
mcqs.explanation: LLM judges have real, known biases (length, confident tone) that don't track true quality, so scores need calibration against a human-labeled sample rather than blind trust — this doesn't mean judges are useless, just that they need oversight. The bias isn't tied specifically to judge model size, and reverting to reference-based metrics wouldn't fix it since those have their own separate weaknesses.

mcqs.question: Why should every real production failure discovered in an LLM system be added to the golden test set?
options: So the exact same regression can be automatically caught before it ships again, rather than silently slipping through a second time
Because golden test sets are required to contain only failure cases, never successful examples
Because it reduces the total number of test cases needed
Because it eliminates the need for online evals entirely
mcqs.explanation: Adding real failures to the golden set closes the loop — a known regression becomes a permanent, automated check rather than something only caught by luck or manual review. Golden sets should mix successful and failing examples, adding cases increases rather than reduces the set's size, and online evals still catch issues golden sets never anticipated.
